evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with generalised anxiety disorder: identification, assessment, stepped care from education to specialist care, psychological and drug treatment, monitoring and non-response. Verified against NICE CG113 and FDA labels; no Saudi guideline found; SFDA not checked. Medicine-pathway restructure on 2026-10-18: medicines regrouped into branches, steps and give-all vs choose-one options; no dose, source or clinical claim was re-checked.
findings: NICE CG113 sections 1.1 and 1.2 (GAD) were read in full on 13 Oct 2026; the panic disorder section was out of scope. Doses and contraindications were read from US FDA labels via openFDA on the same date.
CG113 is a UK guideline; its regulatory references (MHRA, Misuse of Drugs Act) do not apply in Saudi Arabia.
Investigation tiers and added tests were checked against the cited source sections on 15 Oct 2026; additions are pending clinician review.

Medicine list restructured into a branched decision pathway on 2026-10-18. Doses, routes, adjustments, monitoring, contraindications and sources are unchanged from authoring-standard-2026-10-15-v2-investigations-live.

pathophysiology.summary: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is an anxiety disorder in which a person has anxiety or significant worry, often repeated worry about many different issues, and may seek reassurance about physical symptoms. NICE CG113 does not define GAD by symptom count or duration; it advises assessment of distress and functional impairment as well as symptoms. This topic covers GAD in adults, not panic disorder.
keyMechanisms: Diagnosis should not rely solely on the number, severity and duration of symptoms; distress and functional impairment are also assessed (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.6).

Comorbid depressive or other anxiety disorder, substance misuse, medical conditions, past mental health disorders and past treatment response may have affected development, course and severity (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.7).
Substance misuse can be a complication of GAD; harmful and dependent misuse should be treated first (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.9).
Some physical symptoms in people who attend primary care frequently may be due to GAD (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.4–1.2.5).
CG113 does not describe the neurobiology of GAD.

references.title: NICE CG113: Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management
references.edition: NICE guideline, published 26 January 2011, last updated 15 June 2020, Recommendations 1.2.4–1.2.7 and 1.2.9

symptoms: Anxiety or significant worry, and difficulty stopping or controlling worry (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.2 and 1.2.4).
Repeated worrying about many different issues (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.4).
Seeking reassurance about somatic symptoms or a chronic physical health problem, particularly in older people and people from minority ethnic groups (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.4).
Frequent attendance in primary care (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.4).
Distress and functional impairment, which may be marked (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.6 and 1.2.17).
physicalSigns: CG113 lists no examination signs for GAD; assessment rests on history, distress and functional impairment (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.6).
redFlags: Risk of self-harm or suicide together with severe anxiety and marked functional impairment: consider step 4 referral (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.37).
Self-neglect, significant comorbidity such as substance misuse, personality disorder or complex physical health problems: consider step 4 referral (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.37).
Under 30 years and starting an SSRI or SNRI: increased risk of suicidal thinking and self-harm in a minority (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.30).
Comorbid depression or another anxiety disorder: treat the primary (more severe) disorder first (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.8).
precipitants: Past history of an anxiety disorder or a recent traumatic event (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.2).
A chronic physical health problem (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.4).
Comorbid substance misuse, depression or other anxiety disorder (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.7).
Over-the-counter medicines and preparations may interact with prescribed treatment (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.11).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Treat the more severe, primary disorder first; for depression use the depression guideline (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.8).

differentials.condition: Other anxiety disorder, including obsessive-compulsive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Treat the primary disorder first (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.8).
Covered by a separate part of CG113 (section 1.3), which is outside this topic.

differentials.condition: Substance misuse or drug interaction effects
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Harmful and dependent misuse should be treated first as GAD symptoms may improve; ask about cocaine use when prescribing SSRIs (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.9).

differentials.condition: Anxiety symptoms from a physical health problem
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Consider with the person whether symptoms may be due to GAD when they attend seeking reassurance about physical symptoms (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.5); CG113 lists no specific medical mimics.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: A positive screen prompts fuller assessment; CG113 gives no cut-off score.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Consider using the GAD-2 when asking about anxiety and ability to stop or control worry in someone with risk factors or somatic presentations (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.2).

ruleOut.targetCondition: Thyroid dysfunction presenting with unexplained anxiety
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Suppressed or raised TSH with the corresponding free-hormone pattern
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Consider testing for unexplained anxiety; an abnormal result redirects management to the thyroid pathway. Avoid indiscriminate repeat testing during acute illness.

clinicalManagement.title: Step 1: identify, assess, educate and monitor
actions: Be alert to anxiety disorders, especially with past anxiety disorder, somatic symptoms or recent trauma; consider the GAD-2 (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.2).
Identify and communicate the diagnosis early (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.3).
Do a full assessment covering distress, functional impairment, comorbidity, substance use and past treatments (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.6–1.2.7).
Treat a more severe comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder first, and harmful or dependent substance misuse first (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.8–1.2.9).
Give education about GAD and treatment options and actively monitor symptoms and functioning, which may improve less severe presentations (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.10).
Discuss over-the-counter medicines and their interaction risks (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Step 2: low-intensity psychological intervention
actions: Offer one or more of individual non-facilitated self-help, individual guided self-help or psychoeducational groups, guided by preference (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.12).
Non-facilitated self-help: CBT-based materials worked through over at least 6 weeks with minimal contact (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.13).
Guided self-help: CBT-based, usually 5 to 7 weekly or fortnightly sessions of 20 to 30 minutes (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.14).
Psychoeducational groups: usually 6 weekly 2-hour sessions with about 12 participants per therapist (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.15).

clinicalManagement.title: Step 3: high-intensity psychological treatment or drug treatment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Marked impairment or inadequate response to step 2
actions: Offer either an individual high-intensity psychological intervention or drug treatment, explaining benefits and drawbacks including side effects and withdrawal; base the choice on preference (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.17).
Check for risk and comorbidity at each review and consider step 4 if criteria are met (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.37).
Offer CBT or applied relaxation, usually 12 to 15 weekly sessions of 1 hour (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.18–1.2.20).
Offer an SSRI; consider sertraline first as most cost-effective, noting its off-label use for GAD in the UK at publication, with documented informed consent (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.23).

If sertraline is ineffective, offer another SSRI or an SNRI, weighing withdrawal tendency (paroxetine, venlafaxine), side effects, interactions, suicide risk and overdose toxicity (especially venlafaxine) and prior experience (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.24).
If SSRIs and SNRIs are not tolerated, consider pregabalin after assessing for a history of drug abuse (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.25).
Do not offer a benzodiazepine except as a short-term measure in crises, and do not offer an antipsychotic in primary care (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.26–1.2.27).

Explain benefits, side effects, withdrawal, activation (increased anxiety, agitation, poor sleep), the 1 week or longer to full effect, and the need to continue after remission (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.28).
Consider a gastroprotective drug when the bleeding risk with an SSRI is raised, for example in older people or with NSAIDs or aspirin (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.29).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitoring drug treatment
actions: Under 30: warn about suicidal thinking and self-harm risk, see within 1 week, and monitor weekly for the first month (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.30).
For early side effects, monitor closely if mild, reduce the dose, or stop and offer an alternative drug or high-intensity psychological intervention (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.31).
Review effectiveness and side effects every 2 to 4 weeks for 3 months, then every 3 months (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.32).
If effective, continue for at least a year because relapse is likely (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.33).

clinicalManagement.title: Inadequate response
actions: No response to a full course of high-intensity psychological intervention: offer drug treatment (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.34).
No response to drug treatment: offer a high-intensity psychological intervention or an alternative drug (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.35).
Partial response to drug treatment: consider adding a high-intensity psychological intervention (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.36).

Step 4 (specialist) for severe anxiety with marked impairment and risk, comorbidity, self-neglect or inadequate response: specialist assessment of needs and risks, a shared care plan, and only expert-led combination or augmentation, because evidence is lacking and side effects and interactions are more likely (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.37–1.2.42).

guidelineComparison.note: The sources differ in what they prefer rather than contradict on facts; Saudi SFDA registration of each drug for GAD was not checked. Follow the local formulary and specialist advice.

learningObjectives: Identify GAD and apply stepped care from education to specialist care.
Choose between high-intensity psychological and drug treatment with the patient.
Prescribe and monitor SSRIs and SNRIs safely, including in people under 30.
pitfalls: Giving a benzodiazepine other than as a short-term crisis measure (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.26).
Offering an antipsychotic for GAD in primary care (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.27).
Missing the 1-week review and weekly monitoring in under-30s starting an SSRI or SNRI (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.30).
Ignoring SSRI bleeding risk with NSAIDs or aspirin (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.29).
Treating GAD first when a more severe depressive disorder is present (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.8).
keyPoints: Offer the least intrusive, most effective intervention first.
Treat a more severe comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder, and harmful substance misuse, first.
CBT and applied relaxation: usually 12 to 15 weekly hour-long sessions.
First drug: an SSRI, with sertraline considered first; review every 2 to 4 weeks for 3 months.
Continue effective drug treatment for at least a year.

FDA label: Duloxetine delayed-release capsules (set ID 00628e5e-4c5b-2573-e063-6294a90a0e3b)

patientEducation: Provide education about GAD and treatment options, and use NICE's public information (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.10).
Explain the benefits and drawbacks of psychological and drug treatment, including side effects and withdrawal syndromes (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.17).
Explain SSRI and SNRI activation (more anxiety, agitation, poor sleep), the 1 week or more to full effect, and the need to continue after remission (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.28).
Discuss over-the-counter medicines and interactions (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.11).
Address fears about addiction and medication (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.46).
lifestyleAndDiet: CG113 gives no lifestyle or dietary recommendation for GAD; it advises discussing over-the-counter preparations (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.11).
mdtReferrals: Trained practitioners for guided self-help, psychoeducational groups, CBT or applied relaxation (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.14–1.2.21).
Step 4 specialist mental health services for the criteria in NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.37.
Substance misuse services where harmful or dependent misuse is present (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.9).
dischargeCriteria: CG113 sets no discharge criteria; drug treatment continues for at least a year when effective (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.33).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review drug treatment every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months and every 3 months thereafter (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.32). Under 30s see within 1 week and have weekly risk monitoring for a month (NICE CG113 Rec. 1.2.30). Practitioners use routine outcome measures with the person throughout psychological treatment (NICE CG113 Recs 1.2.16 and 1.2.21).
